questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A costume note and what it signals
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a costume note signals.
questions.stem: The costume note beside the harbourmaster's coat reads 'salt-stained, button missing'. What does such a note signal?

options.text: A history of use on the character, whether or not the audience names it.
An instruction that the actor must avoid touching the coat during the scene.
options.misconception: reads a descriptive note as a handling instruction

options.text: A warning that the costume is being used for a different role entirely.
options.misconception: treats a detail as evidence of a casting change

options.text: A note that the costume will be changed before the second act begins.
options.misconception: assumes the note is a scheduling instruction

questions.explanation: A costume note records a garment's state, and a missing button implies a history for the wearer that the audience may read without being told. It is evidence in plain sight.
questions.hint: Ask what the detail is doing for the character.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A property tested under pressure
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a property is tested.
questions.stem: The fountain pen used as a prop was dropped in rehearsal and the cap cracked. Explain why a prop is tested.

answer.exemplar: A prop is tested because it has to work at the moment the plot needs it, and the rehearsal floor is where that truth comes out. A cracked cap leaks ink, and ink on a script, a costume, or a stage floor is not in the plot. Testing shows whether an object can survive being handled, dropped, hidden, and used at speed, and it also reveals the moments when the audience will be watching it closely.

questions.explanation: A prop must work when the plot calls for it, and testing reveals whether it survives handling and speed without spoiling the scene. A cracked cap fails at the wrong moment.
questions.hint: Think about what happens if it fails.

options.text: To withhold information from the audience at a chosen moment.
To show the audience that the production's lighting is well managed.
options.misconception: reads the cue as a display of technical skill

options.text: To cover the moment when a performer steps out of the light.
options.misconception: suggests the cue hides a technical mishap

questions.explanation: The cue controls what the audience can know: dropping the light withholds a character's identity at that moment, directing attention and expectation. It is not a display of lighting skill.
questions.hint: Ask what the audience is prevented from seeing.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A sound cue across a transition
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a sound cue carries a transition.

stimulus.body: At the end of the harbour scene we let the filtration pumps run under the applause. By the time the tanks had been quiet for two seconds, the audience had stopped clapping and was listening for the sea, which was the point: the aquarium's real noise became the next scene.

questions.stem: What does the entry tell us about the sound cue?

options.text: That the sound cue was intended to cover the applause entirely.
options.misconception: reduces the cue to covering applause

options.text: That the production preferred recorded sound to the building's own noise.
options.misconception: invents a preference for recorded sound

options.text: That the cue used the building's real noise to carry the transition.
That the sound of the pumps was unplanned and left in by mistake.
options.misconception: treats a deliberate effect as an accident

questions.explanation: The entry shows the cue deliberately using the pumps' noise so the audience listens for the sea, which carried the transition. It is the opposite of covering applause.
questions.hint: Read the pumps as part of the effect.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A convention the audience has stopped seeing
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an unnoticed convention still works.
questions.stem: A play has ended each act by dimming the lights slowly for thirty years. Explain what has happened to that convention.

answer.exemplar: A repeated convention gradually becomes invisible, and that is what has happened here: the audience no longer reads the slow dim as a signal to settle. It now passes as the natural end of an act, which means it can be used against expectation. If the company suddenly cut the lights instead, the audience would notice the change, and the old convention would become visible again.

questions.explanation: Repetition has made the slow dim invisible, so the audience takes it for granted instead of reading it as a signal. Invisible conventions still work, and breaking one makes it visible again.
questions.hint: Ask what happens when the habit is broken.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The criteria behind a notice
questions.learningObjective: Explain what standards a public notice sets.
questions.stem: The aquarium theatre group's notice lists the rules for the auditorium. Explain what such a notice's criteria are.

answer.exemplar: A public notice states the conditions under which an organisation will operate, and its criteria are practical rather than artistic: safety, access, timing, and what the group can promise in return. It tells a reader what will be provided and what is asked of them, and it is written to be enforceable, which is why it names specific times and duties rather than qualities of the work.

questions.explanation: A notice's criteria are practical conditions of operation: safety, access, timing, and what the group will provide. It is enforceable rather than evaluative, so it names duties and times.
questions.hint: Ask what such a notice is written to do.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A lighting cue and withheld information
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a lighting cue withholds information.
questions.stem: A cue darkens the auditorium before a character speaks in the dark. Explain what that cue does.

answer.exemplar: A cue that darkens the room before a character speaks in darkness withholds the audience's usual visual advantage. Unable to see the speaker, the audience must rely on the voice, the direction of the sound, and what they have been told, and the uncertainty is deliberate rather than a fault in the lighting. The cue therefore shapes what can be known and when.

questions.explanation: The cue deliberately removes the audience's visual advantage so they rely on sound and memory, making the uncertainty part of the design rather than a fault. It controls what can be known.
questions.hint: Ask what the audience loses at that moment.

questions.topic: A costume note and what it signals
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a costume note records.
questions.stem: The aquarium's play uses an oilskin coat that is one size too large. Explain what the note would say about it.

answer.exemplar: A costume note describes the garment as the audience will meet it, and an oversized oilskin tells them something before a word is spoken: that the wearer is larger than the role requires, that the coat was chosen for weather or haste, or that the character is being swallowed by the work. questions.explanation: A costume note records what the garment will suggest to the audience, so an oversized coat becomes a stated reading rather than an accident of fit. It protects the intent from being lost.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A verdict separated from its reasoning
questions.learningObjective: Explain why separate claims in a review differ in kind.
questions.stem: A notice criticises the lighting and then praises the acting. Explain why the two claims are different in kind.

answer.exemplar: The two claims use different criteria and answer to different kinds of evidence. The lighting can be judged against the demands of the text and the visibility of the scene, while the acting is judged against what the roles require of the performers. Separating them matters because a production can be faulted in one register and praised in another, and the reader needs to know which fault and which praise are being offered.

questions.explanation: Lighting and acting are judged against different demands and evidence, so a fault in one does not cancel a praise in the other. Merging them loses the distinction between failure and success.
questions.hint: Ask what each claim is measured against.

questions.explanation: The notebook keeps each garment's state reproducible across a run, so a look achieved on one night can be repeated. It protects accumulated wear as part of the design, not to accident.
questions.hint: Ask what the record makes possible.
